question: A knowledge-management lead has asked Claude three times for a "brief, on-brand" summary of the weekly internal newsletter, and each attempt comes back at a different length and in a different register. Which two revisions to her prompt are most likely to fix this? Select two.
options: A) Replace "brief" with a checkable limit: no more than 150 words in three bullets.
B) Paste one past summary the team accepted and one it rejected, with a note on why.
C) Ask for a more formal register, since inconsistency usually reads as informality.
D) Resend the identical request with a line saying the earlier attempts fell short.
E) Restate the same two adjectives across a longer sentence to give them more weight.
correct_answers: A) Replace "brief" with a checkable limit: no more than 150 words in three bullets.
B) Paste one past summary the team accepted and one it rejected, with a note on why.
explanations: Correct. "Brief" is interpreted afresh each time, which is exactly why the length keeps moving. A word count and a bullet count are constraints Claude can meet and she can verify at a glance.

Correct, and independently of the word limit: it fixes register rather than length. "On-brand" is undefined in the abstract, and a worked accepted-versus-rejected pair shows the voice she means far better than any adjective.
Formality is one register among several, not a cure for varying between registers. She would be swapping an undefined target for a slightly narrower undefined target, and length would still drift.

Resending the same wording with a complaint attached communicates nothing new about what the summary should look like. Repeating a prompt with added emphasis is the classic non-fix for a vague specification.
Expanding "brief" and "on-brand" into more words leaves both terms exactly as unmeasurable as before. Length of instruction is not the same thing as precision of instruction.
